B. SKR Performance Optimization
The impact of UAV hovering-induced misalignment can be
alleviated by sensing-aided tracking. In other words, longer
sensing time of ts enhances the pointing accuracy. This,
in turn, reduces SKR performance due to the shorter time
dedicated to the QKD phase. This trade-off indicates the
existence of an optimal ts. To this end, this study aims to
maximize the SKR performance by allocating the optimal
sensing time resource of ts.
Remark 2. The SKR defined in (8) incorporates several com-
plicated functions, i.e., the Shannon entropy function, the error
function, and Gauss-Hermite quadratures. Therefore, directly
maximizing this SKR using (8) is analytically intractable and
requires extensive computational resources.
We propose a computationally efficient surrogate objective
function capable of capturing the competing factors of this
trade-off, i.e.,

The optimal ts values determined by Brent’s optimization
are denoted by star markers, with colors corresponding to their
respective curves. As seen, the SKR curves are unimodal,
and highly dependent on the sensing time ts. Notably, the
theoretical optimal ts markers closely coincide with the peaks
of the SKR curves. Furthermore, Monte Carlo simulations
show a strong agreement with the analytical lines in all sce-
narios, validating the correctness of the proposed mathematical
framework.
Figure 2 highlights the importance of selecting a proper
beam waist and sensing time. When the sensing time is
below 200 ms, large pointing errors occur nearly disable
QKD transmission. As ts exceeds 200 ms, the QBER curves
become more stable indicating that enhancing the channel
cannot tolerate the impact of hardware limitations. At the
same time, the SKR increases to a peak when the channel
transmittance improves. After that, the SKR decreases because
a long sensing duration reduces the available time for the
quantum phase. Moreover, the results confirm the necessity
of using a narrow beam in QKD as a broader beam reduces
misalignment errors but increases geometric losses. Specifi-
cally, the maximum SKR for a narrow beam with w0 = 10 cm
reaches close to 1 Mbps, while a broader beam at w0 = 30 cm
achieves a peak of under 0.4 Mbps. An increase in w0 enlarges
the beam footprint and makes the system more robust against
angular deviations. The optimal ts shifts to the left. This shows
that the system will conduct less sensing and allocate more
time to the QKD phase to maximize the final SKR.
Table. II compares Brent’s method against the exhaustive
search (baseline) in terms of runtime and accuracy. For the
exhaustive search, 10 000 ts samples are generated within the
range of 10 ms to 1000 ms. When operating on the Gauss-
Hermite based function, Brent’s method reduces the runtime
compared to the baseline exhaustive search while achieving ap-
proximately identical accuracy. Furthermore, applying Brent’s
method to the proposed surrogate function further accelerates
the computation by approximately 7 times compared to its
execution on the Gauss-Hermite function. Notably, the optimal
ts derived from the surrogate model exhibits only a slight
deviation (≈3 ms) compared to the Gauss-Hermite model,
yielding an approximate SKR retention of 99.99%.
Figure 3a illustrates the impact of increasing link distance
Z on the system performance. An increase in Z reduces the
received signal power due to atmospheric attenuation, and
geometric misalignment loss. Specifically, a long transmission
distance causes any given transmitting angle error to create
a larger radial displacement (rd) at the receiver. To mititage
this impairment, the system must increase sensing accuracy by
allocating a larger time amount for the sensing process. For
this reason, the optimal ts increases at longer distances.
Figure 3b illustrates the severe impact of UAV hovering
fluctuations (σf) on the SKR and the optimal sensing time
allocation. Predictably, when the UAV vibrations become
more intense (i.e., σf increases from 100 µrad to 500 µrad),
the maximum achievable SKR drops significantly. Also, the
figure reveals a counter-intuitive behavior regarding resource
allocation, under highly unstable conditions (larger σf), the
optimal sensing time ts notably shifts to the left. Specifi-
cally, the optimal ts decreases from approximately 480 ms
at σf = 100 µrad to around 210 ms at σf = 500 µrad. This
adaptation occurs because, under severe inherent vibrations,
the pointing accuracy is strictly bounded by the hardware
instability. In such scenarios, prolonging the sensing duration
marginally enhance tracking performance. Consequently, the

system adapts by allocating more time for the QKD phase.
V. CONCLUSIONS
This paper has comprehensively investigated the perfor-
mance of a time-constrained sensing-assisted FSO/QKD sys-
tem over realistic FSO quantum channels. We newly derived
mathematical expressions for key performance metrics, i.e.
the QBER and SKR of the decoy-state BB84 protocol. Fur-
thermore, an optimization strategy to maximize the system’s
performance via optimal sensing time allocation was provided.
The accuracy of the proposed analytical framework was rigor-
ously verified through Monte Carlo simulations. The numerical
results offer meaningful insights into system configuration,
highlighting the crucial trade-off between tracking accuracy
and quantum transmission time. Moreover, our contributions
can be expanded for one-way dynamic QKD deployment.
Future work will extend this framework to investigate dynamic
adaptive beam waist optimization and include comprehensive
comparisons against alternative schemes, e.g. MRR-aided sys-
tems.
